llm: Large Language Model - an AI trained on huge text to predict the next word.
rag: Retrieval-Augmented Generation - the model looks up documents before answering.
token: A small chunk of text (about 3/4 of a word) that models read and write.
prompt: The instruction or question you give to an AI model.
agent: An AI that can decide to use tools in a loop to finish a task.
lora: Low-Rank Adaptation - a cheap way to fine-tune a big model with few extra weights.
mcp: Model Context Protocol - a standard way to connect AI apps to tools and data.
hallucination: When an AI confidently says something that is false.
fine-tuning: Training an existing model more on your own data for a specific job.
embedding: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of text.
adversarial distillation attack: An attack where someone secretly tampers with how a small model learns from a bigger one, so the small model picks up bad behavior.
agi: Artificial General Intelligence - a hoped-for AI that can learn and reason across almost any task as well as a human or better.
agentic ai: AI that works like an agent: it plans steps, uses tools and adjusts based on results to finish a goal with little human help.
ai alignment: Making sure an AI's goals and behavior match what humans actually intend and value.
ai benchmarks: Standard tests used to score and compare AI models on tasks like coding, maths or answering questions.
ai fluency: Knowing how to work well and responsibly with AI: what it can do, where it fails, and how to check its output.
ai safety: The field that works to keep AI systems reliable and harmless, even when they are powerful or used in unexpected ways.
ai tech stack: All the hardware, software and compute layers needed to build, train and run AI, from chips up to apps.
ai workflow: The full journey of an AI project: collect data, prepare it, train, test, deploy and maintain the model.
algorithm: A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem, like a recipe.
algorithmic monoculture: When many organizations use the same or very similar AI models or data, so they all make the same mistakes.
artificial hivemind: A group of AI agents that share information and coordinate so they act almost like one system.
artificial intelligence: The science of building machines that can do tasks needing human-like intelligence. The term was coined by John McCarthy in 1955.
attention mechanism: A neural network technique that lets the model focus on the most important parts of the input.
automation: Technology doing a fixed task exactly as humans told it to, without deciding the goal itself.
backpropagation: How a neural network learns from errors: it works backward to find which weights caused the mistake and adjusts them.
bayesian networks: Diagrams that show how different fsactors affect each other using probabilities.
bias in ai: When an AI system's results unfairly favor or harm certain groups of people.
big data: Datasets so large that normal tools can't handle them, so AI is used to find patterns in them.
chatbot: A program that talks with people through text or voice.
closed source: Software whose code is private, so the public can't see, change or reuse it. Also called proprietary.
computer vision: The area of AI that lets computers understand images and videos.
context window: How much text or input an AI model can read and keep in mind at one time.
contrastive learning: Training a model by showing it similar and different pairs so it learns what makes things alike.
data augmentation: Making more training data by creating changed copies of existing data, such as flipped or rotated images.
data mining: Searching large datasets with statistics and machine learning to discover useful patterns.
data poisoning: An attack where someone sneaks bad or mislabeled data into a model's training set to corrupt it.
decision tree: A model that predicts by asking a series of yes/no questions until it reaches an answer.
deep learning: Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn complex patterns.
diffusion models: Generative models that make images by learning to remove noise step by step until a clear picture appears.
dimensionality reduction: Simplifying data by cutting down the number of features while keeping the important information.
ensemble methods: Combining several models so their joint prediction is more accurate than any single one.
ethical ai: Building and using AI in ways that are fair, transparent and good for society.
expert systems: Older AI programs that copy a human expert's decisions using a set of if-then rules.
explainable ai: XAI - methods that make an AI's decisions understandable to humans instead of a black box.
federated learning: Training one model across many devices while the data stays on each device and is never collected centrally.
few-shot learning: When a model learns a new task from only a handful of examples.
foundation models: Huge models trained on broad data that can be adapted to many different tasks.
frontier model: One of the most advanced, general-purpose AI models at the cutting edge right now.
generative ai: AI that creates new content such as text, images, music, code or video.
gans: Generative Adversarial Networks - two networks compete: one makes fake data, the other tries to spot fakes, so both improve.
gpt: Generative Pre-trained Transformer - a family of language models built on the transformer design that generate text.
gpu: Graphics Processing Unit - a chip that does many calculations in parallel, which makes it ideal for training AI.
human-centered ai: An approach to AI that puts human needs, values and well-being first.
hci: Human-Computer Interaction - the study of how people use and interact with computers.
human-in-the-loop: An AI setup where a human checks, corrects or approves the AI's work as part of the process.
hyperparameter: A setting you choose before training, like learning rate or number of layers. The model does not learn it.
hyperscaler: A huge cloud company with massive data centers that can scale computing fast, like AWS, Azure or Google Cloud.
inference: Using a trained model to make predictions on new data.
interpretability: How well humans can understand why an AI model made a decision.
k-nn: k-Nearest Neighbors - classifies something by looking at the k most similar examples it already knows.
knowledge distillation: Training a small student model to copy the outputs of a bigger teacher model.
knowledge graph: A database that stores facts as connected entities and their relationships.
latent space: A compressed hidden space where a model stores the key features of data as numbers.
llmops: Practices for running, monitoring and updating LLM apps in production.
loss function: A formula that measures how wrong a model's predictions are. Training tries to make it smaller.
machine learning: AI that learns patterns from data instead of being given fixed rules.
markov chain: A model where the next step depends only on the current state, not on the full history.
mlops: Practices that combine ML and DevOps to deploy, monitor and maintain models reliably.
model: A mathematical representation, learned from data, used to make predictions.
model drift: When a model gets worse over time because real-world data has changed since training.
multimodal ai: AI that can handle several data types together, such as text, images, audio and video.
nlp: Natural Language Processing - the area of AI that helps computers understand and generate human language.
neural network: A model made of layers of connected artificial neurons, loosely inspired by the brain.
optimization algorithm: A method, like gradient descent, that adjusts a model's weights to reduce mistakes.
overfitting: When a model memorizes training data, including its noise, and then performs poorly on new data.
open-source model: An AI model whose weights, code, training-data details and tools are all shared so anyone can study and rebuild it.
open-weight model: An AI model whose trained weights are public to download, even if the training data or code isn't.
open source: Software whose code is freely available for anyone to view, use and modify.
parameter: A value inside a model that is learned during training, such as a weight.
predictive analytics: Using data and models to forecast future outcomes or trends.
prompt engineering: Writing and refining prompts carefully to get better outputs from an AI model.
prompt injection: An attack where hidden or malicious text tricks an LLM into ignoring its instructions.
reasoning model: An AI model that works through problems step by step before giving its final answer.
reinforcement learning: Learning by trial and error: an agent takes actions and gets rewards or penalties.
responsible ai: The rules and practices that guide safe and ethical AI development and use.
robotics: Building machines that do physical tasks, now often powered by AI.
spatial intelligence: The ability to understand 3D space: where objects are, how they move and how they interact.
self-supervised learning: Training where the model creates its own practice tasks from raw data, like guessing a hidden word.
semantic analysis: Working out the meaning of language from how words and phrases relate.
scaling laws: Patterns showing that AI performance improves predictably as model size, data and compute grow.
supervised learning: Training a model on examples that already have the correct answers (labels).
synthetic data: Data generated by computers or simulations instead of collected from the real world.
tensor: A multi-dimensional container of numbers, like a spreadsheet with more than two dimensions.
tokenization: Splitting text into tokens (words, word pieces or characters) so a model can process it.
traditional ai: Older AI built on hand-written rules and logic instead of learning from data.
training data: The examples (text, images, audio and so on) used to teach a model.
transfer learning: Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a related task.
transformer: A neural network design that uses attention to look at all parts of the input at once. It is the base of modern LLMs.
turing test: A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950: can a machine chat so well that a human can't tell it from a person?
unsupervised learning: Training on data without labels so the model finds patterns or groups on its own.
vector database: A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the most similar ones.
vision transformer: ViT - a transformer adapted to work on images by splitting them into small patches.
weights: The numbers inside a neural network that set how strongly neurons connect. Training adjusts them.
zero-shot learning: When a model does a task it was never specifically trained on, using only general knowledge.
